claim: Microorganisms swimming through viscous fluids imprint their propulsion mechanisms in the flow fields they generate.
source: Microorganisms swimming through viscous fluids imprint their propulsion mechanisms in the flow fields they generate.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established understanding of microswimmer fluid dynamics.

claim: Strongly confining the microalga Chlamydomonas between two parallel plates inhibits its motility through contact friction with the walls.
source: Here, we show that strongly confining the microalga Chlamydomonas between two parallel plates not only inhibits its motility through contact friction with the walls but also leads, for purely mechanical reasons, to inversion of the surrounding vortex flows.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental measurements of cell speed and trajectory tortuosity.

claim: Strong confinement of Chlamydomonas leads to inversion of the surrounding vortex flows for purely mechanical reasons.
source: Here, we show that strongly confining the microalga Chlamydomonas between two parallel plates not only inhibits its motility through contact friction with the walls but also leads, for purely mechanical reasons, to inversion of the surrounding vortex flows.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental flow field measurements and theoretical modeling.

claim: Vortex flow inversion in strong confinement provides the advantage of enhanced fluid mixing despite higher friction.
source: We argue that this vortex flow inversion provides the advantage of enhanced fluid mixing despite higher friction.
evidence: This claim is supported by velocity correlation analysis and tracer displacement measurements.

claim: Fluid friction governs the functional and mechanical responses of microorganisms which operate at low Reynolds number.
source: Fluid friction governs the functional and mechanical responses of microorganisms which operate at low Reynolds number.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of microorganism fluid dynamics.

claim: Microorganisms have developed drag-based propulsive strategies to swim through viscous fluids.
source: They have exploited this friction and developed drag-based propulsive strategies to swim through viscous fluids (Lauga and Powers, 2009; Pedley and Kessler, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microbial biofilms are examples of strongly confined environments encountered in the natural world.
source: Examples include microbial biofilms, bacteria- and algae-laden porous rocks or soil (Qin et al., 2020; Hoh et al., 2016; Foissner, 1998; Bhattacharjee and Datta, 2019); parasitic infections in crowded blood streams and tissues (Heddergott et al., 2012); and biomechanics experiments using thin films and microfluidic channels (Durham et al., 2009; Denissenko et al., 2012; Jeanneret et al., 2019; Ostapenko et al., 2018; Kurtuldu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanical interaction of microswimmers with confining boundaries alters their motility and flow fields.
source: The mechanical interaction of microswimmers with confining boundaries alters their motility and flow fields (Lauga and Powers, 2009; Brotto et al., 2013; Mathijssen et al., 2016), leading to emergent self-organization in cell–cell coordination (Riedel et al., 2005; Petroff et al., 2015), spatial distribution of cells (Tsang and Kanso, 2016; Rothschild, 1963), and ecological aspects such as energy expenditure, nutrient uptake, fluid mixing, transport, and sensing (Lambert et al., 2013; Pushkin and Yeomans, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is considered a next-generation resource for wastewater remediation and synthesis of biofuel, biocatalysts, and pharmaceuticals.
source: They are considered next-generation resources for wastewater remediation and synthesis of biofuel, biocatalysts, and pharmaceuticals (Hoh et al., 2016; Khan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Extreme confinement between two hard walls has been exploited to induce stress memory in CR cells towards enhanced biomass production and cell viability.
source: Recently, extreme confinement between two hard walls has been exploited to induce stress memory in CR cells towards enhanced biomass production and cell viability (Min et al., 2014; Mikulski and Santos-Aberturas, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell speed decreases significantly with increasing confinement as we go from H30 to H10 cells.
source: We find that the cell speed decreases significantly and the trajectory tortuosity increases with increasing confinement as we go from H30 to H10 cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Trajectory tortuosity increases with increasing confinement as we go from H30 to H10 cells.
source: We find that the cell speed decreases significantly and the trajectory tortuosity increases with increasing confinement as we go from H30 to H10 cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The beat-cycle averaged experimental flow field of strongly confined cells has opposite flow vorticity to that expected from the screened version of bulk flow.
source: Surprisingly, the beat-cycle averaged experimental flow field of strongly confined cells has opposite flow vorticity to that expected from the screened version of bulk flow (Drescher et al., 2010; Guasto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental flow field measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: The vortex flow inversion comes about because the close proximity of the walls greatly suppresses the motility of the organism.
source: This counterintuitive result comes about because the close proximity of the walls greatly suppresses the motility of the organism and, consequently, the thrust force of the flagella is balanced primarily by the non-hydrodynamic contact friction from the walls.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and force balance analysis.

claim: The thrust force of the flagella is balanced primarily by the non-hydrodynamic contact friction from the walls in strong confinement.
source: This counterintuitive result comes about because the close proximity of the walls greatly suppresses the motility of the organism and, consequently, the thrust force of the flagella is balanced primarily by the non-hydrodynamic contact friction from the walls.
evidence: This is an inference based on force balance analysis and experimental observations.

claim: The flagellar thrust is largely unaffected by the walls in strong confinement.
source: The reason being that the flagellar thrust is largely unaffected by the walls, whereas the hydrodynamic drag on the slowly moving cell body is readily seen to be far smaller.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that flagella beat far from the walls and maintain similar beat frequency.

claim: Theoretical predictions from the source-dipole description of strongly confined swimmers do not account for vortex flow inversion because they include only hydrodynamic stresses.
source: Understandably, theoretical predictions from the source-dipole description of strongly confined swimmers do not account for this vortex flow inversion because they include only hydrodynamic stresses (Brotto et al., 2013; Mathijssen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with existing theoretical models cited in the literature.

claim: The net force and torque on microswimmers can be taken to be zero as gravitational effects are negligible in the case of CR for the range of length scales considered.
source: The net force and torque on microswimmers, together with the ambient medium and boundaries, can be taken to be zero as gravitational effects are negligible in the case of CR for the range of length scales considered (Drescher et al., 2010; Brennen and Winet, 1977; Pedley and Kessler, 1992; Elgeti et al., 2015; Mathijssen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: The two local forces exerted by any dipolar microswimmer on the surrounding fluid are flagellar propulsive thrust Fth and cell body drag Fhd.
source: The two local forces exerted by any dipolar microswimmer on the surrounding fluid are flagellar propulsive thrust Fth and cell body drag Fhd.
evidence: This is established knowledge in microswimmer mechanics.

claim: Flagellar thrust and cell body drag balance each other completely for any swimmer in an unbounded medium.
source: They balance each other completely for any swimmer in an unbounded medium (Lauga and Powers, 2009; Goldstein, 2015) and approximately in weak confinement between two hard walls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CR is a classic example of an active puller where the cell draws in fluid along the propulsion axis and ejects it in the perpendicular plane.
source: In these regimes, CR is the classic example of an active puller where the direction of force dipole due to thrust and drag are such that the cell draws in fluid along the propulsion axis (x-axis in Figure 1A) and ejects it in the perpendicular plane (Lauga and Powers, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CR swimming mechanics supported by citation.

claim: CR is described well by three point forces or Stokeslets because the thrust is spatially extended and distributed equally between the two flagella.
source: CR is described well by three point forces or Stokeslets (Drescher et al., 2010) as in Figure 1A because the thrust is spatially extended and distributed equally between the two flagella.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In strong confinement, the flagellar thrust is balanced by the combined drag due to the cell body and the strongly confining walls.
source: Therefore, the flagellar thrust is balanced by the combined drag due to the cell body and the strongly confining walls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on force balance analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: As confinement increases, the drag on the cells due to the solid walls increases and they trace out smaller distances with increasing twists and turns in the trajectory.
source: As confinement increases, the drag on the cells due to the solid walls increases and they trace out smaller distances with increasing twists and turns in the trajectory (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The H30 flow field shows standard features of an unbounded CR's flow field, namely far-field four-lobe flow of a puller, two lateral vortices at 8–9 μm from cell's major axis, and anterior flow along the swimming direction till a stagnation point, 21 μm from the cell centre.
source: It shows standard features of an unbounded CR's flow field (Drescher et al., 2010; Guasto et al., 2010), namely far-field four-lobe flow of a puller, two lateral vortices at 8–9 μm from cell's major axis, and anterior flow along the swimming direction till a stagnation point, 21 μm from the cell centre (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental flow field measurements shown in Figure 3A and B, compared with cited literature.

claim: The vortices contributing dominantly to the flow in strongly confined geometry are opposite in sign to those in the bulk or weakly confined case.
source: Strikingly, the vortices contributing dominantly to the flow in this strongly confined geometry are opposite in sign to those in the bulk (Drescher et al., 2010) or weakly confined case (H30, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental flow field measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The two-lobed flow in strong confinement is distinct from expectations based on the screened version of the bulk or three-Stokeslet flow, which is four-lobed.
source: This two-lobed flow is distinct from expectations based on the screened version of the bulk or three-Stokeslet flow, which is four-lobed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison between experimental data and theoretical predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The far-field flow of strongly confined CR resembles a 2D source dipole pointing opposite to the swimmer's motion.
source: Importantly, the far-field flow resembles a 2D source dipole pointing opposite to the swimmer's motion, which is entirely different from that produced by the standard source dipole theory of strongly confined swimmers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Brotto et al., 2013; Mathijssen et al., 2016; Jeanneret et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental flow field measurements compared with theoretical predictions from cited literature.

claim: The source-dipole treatment does not consider the possibility that the cells are squeezed by the walls, or in other words, it does not account for contact friction.
source: This is because the source-dipole treatment does not consider the possibility that the cells are squeezed by the walls, or in other words, it does not account for contact friction (Brotto et al., 2013; Mathijssen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of existing theoretical models cited in the literature.

claim: The viscous power dissipated through the flow fields is nearly the same for H30 and H10 cells.
source: Even though the flow fields of H30 and H10 cells look strikingly different, the viscous power dissipated through the flow fields is nearly the same (Appendix 1.1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental flow field data.

claim: The large vortices flanking the rapidly moving CR in H30 are shrunken and localized close to the cell body in H10 due to the greatly reduced swimming speed.
source: The large vortices flanking the rapidly moving CR in H30 are shrunken and localized close to the cell body in H10 due to the greatly reduced swimming speed.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of experimental flow fields.

claim: The frontal vortices generated by flagellar motion now fill most of the flow field in H10.
source: The frontal vortices generated by flagellar motion now fill most of the flow field in H10.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental flow field data.

claim: The frontal vortices are generated largely during the power stroke of flagella and are opposite in sense to the vortices produced by the moving cell body.
source: Generated largely during the power stroke of flagella, they are opposite in sense to the vortices produced by the moving cell body.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of flagellar mechanics and flow field observations.

claim: The force balance holds for the case of weak confinement (H30) as well.
source: We assume this balance holds for the case of weak confinement (H30) as well.
evidence: This is an assumption based on established knowledge and the degree of confinement.

claim: The flagellar thrust works mainly against the non-hydrodynamic contact friction from the walls as expected due to the extremely low speed of the strongly confined swimmer.
source: Thus, the flagellar thrust works mainly against the non-hydrodynamic contact friction from the walls as expected due to the extremely low speed of the strongly confined swimmer.
evidence: This is an inference based on force balance analysis.

claim: The theoretical flow of Liron and Mochon decays much more rapidly than the experimental one and does not capture the vortex positions and flow variation in the experiment.
source: However, the theoretical flow of Liron and Mochon decays much more rapidly than the experimental one and does not capture the vortex positions and flow variation in the experiment (Appendix 1.2 and Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The Liron and Mochon approximation to the confined Stokeslet flow is itself singular and also the far-field limit of the full analytical solution, so it cannot be expected to accurately explain the near-field characteristics of the experimental flow.
source: This is because the Liron and Mochon approximation to the confined Stokeslet flow is itself singular and also the far-field limit of the full analytical solution, so it cannot be expected to accurately explain the near-field characteristics of the experimental flow (Liron and Mochon, 1976).
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of the cited theoretical model.

claim: Superposing the Brinkman solution for the conventional three point forces at cell centre and flagellar positions of CR is an inappropriate description of the strongly confined flow.
source: We have already shown that superposing our Brinkman solution for the conventional three point forces at cell centre and flagellar positions of CR, which leads to the effective three-Stokeslet model in 2D, is an inappropriate description of the strongly confined flow (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The cell is nearly stationary compared to the motion of its flagella in strong confinement.
source: This is not surprising at this point because the force imbalance between the flagellar thrust and hydrodynamic cell drag suggests that the cell is nearly stationary compared to the motion of its flagella.
evidence: This is an inference based on force balance analysis and experimental observations.

claim: The theoretical 'two-Stokeslet Brinkman flow' decays faster than the experiment.
source: However, this theoretical 'two-Stokeslet Brinkman flow' (Figure 4A) decays faster than the experiment as shown in the quantitative comparison of these two flows in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The 'two-Gaussian Brinkman flow' with σ~L/2=5 μm has captured the flow variation and most of the experimental flow features accurately.
source: Notably, Figure 4C, that is, the 'two-Gaussian Brinkman flow', has captured the flow variation and most of the experimental flow features accurately.
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The two-Gaussian Brinkman flow has captured the lateral vortices at 20 μm and an anterior stagnation point at 13 μm from cell centre.
source: Specifically, these are the lateral vortices at 20 μm and an anterior stagnation point at 13 μm from cell centre.
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The theoretical model cannot account for the front-back asymmetry of the strongly confined flow.
source: The only limitation of this theoretical model is that it cannot account for the front-back asymmetry of the strongly confined flow, as is evident from Figure 4D for the polar angles 0 or 2π and π which correspond to front and back of the cell, respectively.
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The cell body squashed between the two solid walls mostly blocks the forward flow from reaching the cell posterior.
source: This deviation is more pronounced in the frontal region as the cell body squashed between the two solid walls mostly blocks the forward flow from reaching the cell posterior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometry of the system and flow field observations.

claim: The no-slip boundary on the cell body needs to be invoked to mimic the front-back flow asymmetry.
source: Thus, the no-slip boundary on the cell body needs to be invoked to mimic the front-back flow asymmetry, which is a more involved analysis due to the presence of multiple boundaries and can be addressed in a follow-up study.
evidence: This is a speculation about future theoretical work needed.

claim: The three-Gaussian Brinkman flow for H=30 μm matches qualitatively with the experimental flow field of CR in weak confinement.
source: The resulting flow field (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) matches qualitatively with the experimental flow field of CR in weak confinement (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental data.

claim: The experimental and theoretical flow fields show that the contact friction from the walls reduces the force-dipolar swimmer in bulk or weak confinement (H30) to a force-monopole one in strong confinement (H10).
source: Together, the experimental and theoretical flow fields show that the contact friction from the walls reduces the force-dipolar swimmer in bulk or weak confinement (H30) to a force-monopole one in strong confinement (H10).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on experimental data and theoretical modeling.

claim: The photosynthetic alga CR feeds on dissolved inorganic ions/molecules such as phosphate, nitrogen, ammonium, and carbon dioxide from the surrounding fluid in addition to using sunlight as the major source of energy.
source: The photosynthetic alga CR feeds on dissolved inorganic ions/molecules such as phosphate, nitrogen, ammonium, and carbon dioxide from the surrounding fluid in addition to using sunlight as the major source of energy (Tam and Hosoi, 2011; Kiørboe, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nitrogen and carbon are limiting macronutrients to algal growth and metabolism.
source: Importantly, nitrogen and carbon are limiting macronutrients to algal growth and metabolism (Khan et al., 2018; Short et al., 2006; Kiørboe, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Flagella-generated flow fields help in uniform distribution of dissolved solute molecules through fluid mixing and transport which have a positive influence on the nutrient uptake of osmotrophs like CR.
source: It is widely known that flagella-generated flow fields help in uniform distribution of these dissolved solute molecules through fluid mixing and transport which have a positive influence on the nutrient uptake of osmotrophs like CR (Kiørboe, 2008; Tam and Hosoi, 2011; Ding et al., 2014; Short et al., 2006; Leptos et al., 2009; Kurtuldu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Flow-field-mediated advection does not completely dominate, but nevertheless can play a role in nutrient uptake for small biological molecules along with diffusion-mediated transport, especially for the strongly confined cell.
source: These numbers suggest that flow-field-mediated advection does not completely dominate, but nevertheless can play a role in nutrient uptake for small biological molecules along with diffusion-mediated transport, especially for the strongly confined cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated Péclet numbers.

claim: The H30 swimmers pass through the field of view in ~1-1.4 s.
source: The H30 swimmers are fast and therefore pass through this field of view in ∼1-1.4 s (Figure 5B), whereas the slow-moving H10 swimmers stay in the field of view for the maximum recording time of ∼8 s (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental videos.

claim: The slow-moving H10 swimmers stay in the field of view for the maximum recording time of ~8 s.
source: The H30 swimmers are fast and therefore pass through this field of view in ∼1-1.4 s (Figure 5B), whereas the slow-moving H10 swimmers stay in the field of view for the maximum recording time of ∼8 s (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental videos.

claim: The radius of influence of the H10 flow is higher than the H30 one.
source: That is, the radius of influence of the H10 flow is higher than the H30 one, which corroborates the longer velocity correlation length scale in strong confinement.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tracer displacement data.

claim: The fluid is advected more in strong confinement leading to enhanced fluid mixing and transport.
source: Together, Figure 5 shows that the fluid is advected more in strong confinement leading to enhanced fluid mixing and transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: The opposite vortical flows driven by flagellar beating in strong confinement help in advection-dominated dispersal of nutrients, air and CO2 in the surrounding fluid.
source: In other words, the opposite vortical flows driven by flagellar beating in strong confinement help in advection-dominated dispersal of nutrients, air and CO2 in the surrounding fluid, thereby aiding the organism to avail itself of more nutrients for growth and metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced mixing results.

claim: A prototypical puller-type of microswimmer like CR, when squeezed between two solid walls with a gap that is narrower than its size, has a remarkedly different motility and flow field from those of a bulk swimmer.
source: Our results show that a prototypical puller-type of microswimmer like CR, when squeezed between two solid walls with a gap that is narrower than its size, has a remarkedly different motility and flow field from those of a bulk swimmer.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: In the regime of strong confinement, the cells experience a non-hydrodynamic contact friction that is large enough to decrease their swimming speed by 96%.
source: In this regime of strong confinement, the cells experience a non-hydrodynamic contact friction that is large enough to decrease their swimming speed by 96%.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements and force balance analysis.

claim: The effect of strongly confined cells on the fluid is dominantly through the flagella, which pull the fluid towards the organism.
source: Consequently, their effect on the fluid is dominantly through the flagella, which pull the fluid towards the organism and therefore, the major vortices in the associated flow field have vorticity opposite to that observed in bulk or weak confinement.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental flow field observations and force balance analysis.

claim: The major vortices in the flow field of strongly confined cells have vorticity opposite to that observed in bulk or weak confinement.
source: Consequently, their effect on the fluid is dominantly through the flagella, which pull the fluid towards the organism and therefore, the major vortices in the associated flow field have vorticity opposite to that observed in bulk or weak confinement.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental flow field measurements.

claim: The vortex inversion leads to an increased mixing and transport through the flow in strong confinement.
source: This leads to an increased mixing and transport through the flow in strong confinement.
evidence: This is based on velocity correlation and tracer displacement analyses.

claim: These experimental results arise due to mechanical friction from the walls and not due to any behavioural change.
source: These experimental results, which arise due to mechanical friction from the walls and not due to any behavioural change, establish that confinement not only alters the hydrodynamic stresses but also modifies the swimmer motility which in turn impacts the fluid flows.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and force balance analysis.

claim: Confinement not only alters the hydrodynamic stresses but also modifies the swimmer motility which in turn impacts the fluid flows.
source: These experimental results, which arise due to mechanical friction from the walls and not due to any behavioural change, establish that confinement not only alters the hydrodynamic stresses but also modifies the swimmer motility which in turn impacts the fluid flows.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The coupling between confinement and motility is typically ignored in theoretical studies because the focus tends to be on the effect of confining geometry on flow fields induced by a given set of force generators.
source: This coupling between confinement and motility is typically ignored in theoretical studies because the focus tends to be on the effect of confining geometry on flow fields induced by a given set of force generators (Brotto et al., 2013; Mathijssen et al., 2016), which is appropriate for weak confinement, whereas strong confinement alters the complexion of forces generating the flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of cited theoretical literature.

claim: The theoretical approach of using two like-signed Brinkman Stokeslets localized with a Gaussian spread on the propelling appendages can be easily utilized to analyze flows of a dilute collection of strongly confined swimmers.
source: Our theoretical approach of using two like-signed Brinkman Stokeslets localized with a Gaussian spread on the propelling appendages can also be easily utilized to analyze flows of a dilute collection of strongly confined swimmers (Appendix 1.6 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the theoretical approach.

claim: The force-monopolar flow field of the strongly confined CR is similar to that of tethered microorganisms like Vorticella within the slide-coverslip experimental setup.
source: Notably, the force-monopolar flow field of the strongly confined CR is similar to that of tethered microorganisms like Vorticella within the slide-coverslip experimental setup (Pepper et al., 2009; O'Malley, 2011).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: The effective 2D theoretical model involving Brinkman Stokeslet is applicable to tethered microorganisms like Vorticella.
source: Therefore, our effective 2D theoretical model involving Brinkman Stokeslet is applicable to these contexts as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on similarity of flow fields.

claim: One needs to account for the differences in ciliary beating for a comprehensive description of the flow field closer to the organism.
source: However, one needs to account for the differences in ciliary beating (two-ciliary flow for CR whereas multi-ciliated metachronal waves for Vorticella) for a comprehensive description of the flow field closer to the organism (Pepper et al., 2009; Ryu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about necessary modifications for different organisms.

claim: CR is known to glide on liquid-infused solid substrates through flagella-mediated adhesive interactions.
source: We note that even though CR is known to glide on liquid-infused solid substrates through flagella-mediated adhesive interactions (Sasso et al., 2018), it has recently been shown that the strength of flagellar adhesion is sensitive to and switchable by ambient light (Kreis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The strength of flagellar adhesion is sensitive to and switchable by ambient light.
source: We note that even though CR is known to glide on liquid-infused solid substrates through flagella-mediated adhesive interactions (Sasso et al., 2018), it has recently been shown that the strength of flagellar adhesion is sensitive to and switchable by ambient light (Kreis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: It is likely that CR in its natural habitat of rocks and soils would also utilize swimming in addition to gliding.
source: Consequently, it is likely that CR in its natural habitat of rocks and soils would also utilize swimming in addition to gliding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the light-sensitivity of adhesion.

claim: Despite the higher frictional drag due to the strongly confining walls, there is enhanced fluid mixing due to the H10 flow field.
source: Our quantitative analysis shows that despite the higher frictional drag due to the strongly confining walls, there is enhanced fluid mixing due to the H10 flow field.
evidence: This is based on velocity correlation and tracer displacement analyses.

claim: The inverse vortical flows driven by the flagellar propulsive thrust help in advection-mediated transport of nutrients to the strongly confined microswimmer.
source: That is, the inverse vortical flows driven by the flagellar propulsive thrust help in advection-mediated transport of nutrients to the strongly confined microswimmer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced mixing results.

claim: The experimental and theoretical methodologies are completely general and can be applied to any strongly confined microswimmer, biological or synthetic from individual to collective scales.
source: Finally, our experimental and theoretical methodologies are completely general and can be applied to any strongly confined microswimmer, biological or synthetic from individual to collective scales.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the methods.

claim: The description using point or Gaussian forces in a quasi-2D Brinkman equation is simple enough to implement and analyze confined flows in a wide range of active systems.
source: Specifically, our robust and efficient description using point or Gaussian forces in a quasi-2D Brinkman equation is simple enough to implement and analyze confined flows in a wide range of active systems.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the theoretical approach.

claim: This work is expected to inspire further studies on biomechanics and fluid mixing due to hard-wall confinement of concentrated active suspensions.
source: We expect our work to inspire further studies on biomechanics and fluid mixing due to hard-wall confinement of concentrated active suspensions (Kurtuldu et al., 2011; Pushkin and Yeomans, 2014; Jin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: These effects can be exploited in realizing autonomous motion through microchannel for biomedical applications and in microfluidic devices for efficient control, navigation and trapping of microbes and synthetic swimmers.
source: These effects can be exploited in realizing autonomous motion through microchannel for biomedical applications and in microfluidic devices for efficient control, navigation and trapping of microbes and synthetic swimmers (Park et al., 2017; Karimi et al., 2013; Temel and Yesilyurt, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications supported by citations.

claim: CR cells are synchronously grown in 12:12 hr light:dark cycle in Tris-Acetate-Phosphate (TAP + P) medium.
source: CR cells are synchronously grown in 12:12 hr light:dark cycle in Tris-Acetate-Phosphate (TAP + P) medium.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The TAP + P culture medium contains divalent ions such as Ca2+, Mg2+, SO42- which decrease the screening length of the 200 nm negatively charged microspheres.
source: This culture medium contains divalent ions such as Ca2+, Mg2+, SO42- which decrease the screening length of the 200 nm negatively charged microspheres, thereby promoting inter-particle aggregation and sticking to glass surfaces and CR's flagella.
evidence: This is established knowledge about electrostatic interactions.

claim: The sulfate latex microspheres are sterically stabilized by grafting long polymer chains of polyethylene glycol with the help of a positively charged poly-l-lysine backbone.
source: Therefore, the sulfate latex microspheres (S37491, Thermo Scientific) are sterically stabilized by grafting long polymer chains of polyethylene glycol (mPEG-SVA-20k, NANOCS, USA) with the help of a positively charged poly-l-lysine backbone (P7890, 15–30 kDa, Sigma) (Mondal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol supported by citation.

claim: The coverslip and slide surfaces are cleaned and coated with polyacrylamide brush to prevent non-specific adhesion of microspheres and flagella to the glass surfaces.
source: In addition, the coverslip and slide surfaces are also cleaned and coated with polyacrylamide brush to prevent non-specific adhesion of microspheres and flagella to the glass surfaces, prior to sample injection (Mondal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol supported by citation.

claim: The sample chamber is placed under red light illumination (>610 nm) to prevent adhesion of flagella and phototactic response of CR.
source: The sample chamber containing cells and tracers is mounted on an inverted microscope (Olympus IX83/IX73) and placed under red light illumination (>610 nm) to prevent adhesion of flagella (Kreis et al., 2017) and phototactic response of CR (Sineshchekov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol supported by citations.

claim: The measured chamber height for the 10 μm spacer is 10.88 ± 0.68 μm.
source: We find the measured chamber height for the 10 μm spacer to be 10.88 ± 0.68 μm and for the 30 μm spacer to be 30.32 ± 0.87 μm, from eight different samples in each case.
